checks.diagnosis: The prompt allows cuts that leave a verb/copula or preposition that syntactically requires a following complement, producing fragments that read as contradictions or nonsense on their own.
checks.evidence: en_us_378, en_us_44, en_us_688, en_us_119 — each policy cut left a predicate or prepositional head (e.g. "is called the", "is moving towards the", "been removed to the", "Japanese newspaper that they") that required its complement and yielded very high contra.
checks.type_predicate: Positions where the token immediately before the candidate cut is a verb, copula, or preposition that normally requires a syntactic complement (i.e., the preceding fragment would be an incomplete predicate or PP without following words).

edit.text: Do not cut when the token before the marker is a verb/copula or a preposition that syntactically requires a following complement (the fragment would be an incomplete predicate or PP).

orders.diagnosis: When two allowed cuts compete, the prompt prefers earlier cuts that isolate single-word function tokens; this harms short-latency segmentations that must keep function words attached to their content.
orders.evidence: en_us_381, en_us_633, en_us_1116 — in each case the policy favored a cut immediately after a single function word or discourse particle, while the target prefers the later cut that keeps that function word attached to its content.
orders.type_predicate: Pairs of candidate cuts in the same sentence where one cut falls immediately after a single-word function token (a determiner, pronoun, auxiliary or discourse connective) and the other falls later inside the following phrase.

edit.text: When one candidate is immediately after a single-word function token and the other is later inside the following phrase, prefer the later cut (keep the function word attached to its content).
